Source page 1. A fraction describes selected equal parts of the same whole. The denominator names the unit and the numerator counts how many such units are selected. Fractions must refer to the same whole before their quantities can be compared. Equivalent fractions represent the same quantity: multiplying both numerator and denominator by the same positive integer changes the partition without changing the quantity. For example, 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6. To add 1/2 and 1/3 of the same whole, use sixths: 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6. Adding the denominators gives the wrong unit. For positive addends, the sum should be greater than either addend; here it is also less than one whole. A counterexample guards the same-whole condition: half of a small cake need not equal half of a large cake. A drawn model should label the whole and show equal-sized parts. If the original wholes differ, first describe their sizes instead of treating the fractions alone as a sufficient comparison. Check a proposed answer by converting it back into the original quantities. A correct numerical answer with an unexplained unit still needs a reasoning check. Explain what the numerator counts and what unit the denominator names before applying a rule.
